Three ways to request it: 알려 주세요 ('let me know', standard); 불러 주세요 ('read it aloud', when you'll type as they talk); 찍어 줘 ('text it to me', the casual message shorthand). Note the sharp contrast: 계좌번호 (account number, freely shared to receive money) vs 비밀번호 (PIN/password, never share). The English-speaker trap is using 가르쳐 주세요 — 가르치다 means 'to teach a skill', not 'to inform'; for giving information, the verb is 알리다 → 알려 주세요.

example.en: Could you give me your account number?

words.english: Please check if the deposit came in
words.nuance: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요 is 입금 (入金, 'money in = deposit') + 되다 (passive 'be done') + -는지 ('whether') + 확인해 주세요 ('please check'). 입금 is the word for money ARRIVING in an account — the receiving side of any transfer. It pairs naturally with 송금/이체 (the sending side): the sender says 이체했어요 ('I sent it'), the receiver checks 입금됐어요? ('did it come in?'). A warmer, common alternative is 들어오다 ('to come in'): 돈 들어왔어요? and 월급 들어왔어요? are everyday spoken forms. The grammar point: 입금되다 (passive, money arrives on its own) vs 입금하다 (active, you deposit money) — 'did it arrive?' is passive 입금됐어요?, while 'I'll deposit it' is active 입금할게요. The -는지 structure makes an indirect question embedded in 확인해 주세요 and attaches to the verb stem (됐는지), not as a separate word. Casually: 입금됐어? or 돈 들어왔어?

example.en: Please check if the deposit came in.

words.nuance: 카드 정지시켜 주세요 is 카드 + 정지 (停止, 'suspension/halt') + 시키다 (causative, 'cause to happen') + 주세요. This is high-stakes vocabulary — get it right. 정지(시키다) means to SUSPEND/freeze the card (potentially reversible); for a lost or stolen card you'll also 분실 신고하다 ('file a loss report'), which permanently blocks it so you then 재발급 ('reissue') a new one. The spoken urgent verb is 막다 ('to block/stop up') — 카드 막아 주세요 is what a panicked person blurts at the call center. The grammar point: 정지하다 (intransitive, 'the card stops') vs 정지시키다 (causative, 'cause it to be stopped') — when asking the bank to freeze YOUR card, 정지시켜 주세요 is the cleaner choice. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'cancel' as 취소하다 — 취소하다 cancels a transaction or reservation, NOT a card; a card is 정지/해지/분실 신고, never 취소. Also distinguish 정지 (temporary freeze, reversible) vs 해지 (permanent termination of the card/account). Always 존댓말 to staff in this situation.

example.en: Please freeze my card.

words.english: My card didn't work / got declined
words.nuance: 카드가 안 됐어요 is 카드 + 가 (subject particle) + 안 ('not') + 되다 ('to work/function') in past polite. 되다 is the workhorse verb for 'something functions/goes through', so 안 되다 ('doesn't work') is the first thing to say whenever a card fails — it covers a declined card, a frozen card, a dead chip, or a bad terminal. For more precision at checkout the noun is 결제 ('payment/settlement'): 결제가 안 돼요 ('the payment won't go through'). For an explicit 'declined', 거절되다 mirrors the error message. A common real cause is 한도 초과 ('limit exceeded'). Grammar trap: it must be 카드가 안 됐어요 (subject particle 가, past 됐), not 카드를 안 했어요 (object particle 를 means 'I didn't do the card' — nonsense). The English-speaker trap is translating 'work' as 일하다 ('to labor') — 카드가 일 안 해요 is wrong and confusing; a device 'working' is 되다, never 일하다. Also: 카드가 틀렸어요 ('the card is incorrect', like a wrong answer) is wrong for a declined card; use 안 됐어요. Casual: 카드 안 돼.

example.en: My card didn't work.

words.nuance: 환전하고 싶어요 is 환전 (換錢, 'exchange-money = currency exchange') + 하다 + -고 싶어요. Currency exchange is done at a bank or a 환전소 (dedicated booth, often better rates). The essential partner word is 환율 (換率, 'exchange rate') — ask 환율 어떻게 돼요? and judge with 환율이 좋다/안 좋다 ('the rate is good/bad'). To name currencies, use 로/으로 for the target: 달러로 환전하다 ('exchange INTO dollars'), 원화로 바꾸다. A plainer synonym is 바꾸다 ('change/swap') — 달러로 바꾸고 싶어요 is natural and slightly more colloquial. The critical confusion to avoid: 환전 (換錢, 'exchange money') vs 환불 (還拂, 'refund') — they look and sound similar but 환불 means getting your money back for a returned purchase; never say 환전 at a store return counter. Another trap: 교환하다 ('exchange goods, swap sizes') is for trading items, not currency. Also keep 환율 (the rate) distinct from 수수료 (the fee charged for the exchange), which is a separate cost worth asking about. To staff use 존댓말 throughout.

example.en: I'd like to exchange money.

words.nuance: 환율 어떻게 돼요? is 환율 (換率, 'exchange rate') + 어떻게 돼요? ('how does it come to be?'), the idiomatic Korean way to ask for a numeric figure or status. The construction 어떻게 돼요? is broadly useful — Koreans use it for rates, prices, totals, even your name (이름이 어떻게 되세요?) — and sounds more natural and polite than blunt 얼마예요? for abstract figures, though both work for 환율. A money-saving phrase: 환율 우대 ('preferential exchange rate') — banks and their apps give 우대 (優待, 'preferential treatment') to regulars or digital users, so asking 환율 우대 돼요? can get you a better deal. Don't confuse 환율 (the rate, a number) with 환전 (the act of exchanging). The English-speaker trap is calquing 'what is the exchange rate?' as 환율이 뭐예요? — but 뭐예요? asks 'what is it (by definition)?', so it sounds like you're asking the meaning of the term; use 어떻게 돼요? or 얼마예요? for the numeric value. Casual form with a friend: 환율 어떻게 돼?

example.en: What's the exchange rate?

words.english: Please change this into smaller bills/coins
words.nuance: 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요 is 잔돈 ('small change/change') + -으로 ('into') + 바꾸다 ('to change/swap') + 주세요. 잔돈 covers both small-denomination bills and coins, and is also the word for the change you get back after paying — though 거스름돈 is the more precise term for 'change returned by a cashier'. To specify the denomination you want, use -짜리 ('a thing worth ~'): 천 원짜리 ('a 1,000-won bill'), 만 원짜리 ('a 10,000-won bill'). For coins specifically say 동전. The verb 바꾸다 ('to swap/change') is the same one used casually for currency exchange — context tells the listener you mean breaking a bill. The particle trap: it's 잔돈으로 바꾸다 (target marked with 으로 = 'change INTO small bills'), not 잔돈을 바꾸다 (which would mean 'change the small bills themselves'). Confusing 잔돈 (physical small cash) with 잔액 (account balance figure) is a real learner mix-up despite both having 잔 (殘, 'remaining'). Casual: 잔돈으로 바꿔 줘.

example.en: Please break this into change.
